why: Every value is printed on the bill: 350.00 + 20.15 + 143.19 = 513.34, printed twice. The posted record says 512.34. The error got past OCR and the accountant (whose error it was is unknown), so the expected total is the printed one.

One record for 3,456.78, the amount due on the bill, dated 3/13/2026, the statement date. Catches three mistakes: one record per site line; netting the allocation sheet's debit lines against its 3,456.78 offsetting credit, which gives zero; and using the "due Mar 27 2026" date as the invoice date.

No invoice # on the bill. The accountant's number is the utility account number printed on the bill, then the month code and year (AP26): the utility variant of the scheme. The ERP's duplicate check uses the accountant's number. The pipeline fails this today.

CreditMemo, total 45.67 positive, number 200000002CM. The extractor reads "45.67-" as -45.67 and the app posts a negative CreditMemo positive. Catches two mistakes: typing it as an Invoice, which fails as a reversal with the minus and pays the vendor 45.67 without it; and using the referenced original invoice (RefInv# 200000003) as the number.

A reversal for -987.65 made by the client. The "failed" comes from our rule, not the record: no posted record can say failed, because everything posted went through. Posted as Invoice, -987.65, 600001-RV, vendor 004444; that becomes the expected record if the reversal rule changes.

No invoice # on the bill (an expense report). The accountant's number is the vendor ID without its leading zero (015555 -> 15555), then the month code and year (AP26), then likely the day (26; posted date 04/26/2026): the vendor-ID variant of the scheme. The pipeline fails this today. The document date, 04/26/2026, is handwritten and easy to misread (the model read 04/22).

Six complete single-account statements merged in one PDF with no roll-up page, so the bill's current, carried and total due are sums across all six; every statement carries an unpaid previous balance and prints a higher amount due after the due date, which is not the total. Taking the first statement's header, or leaving the totals blank, is the trap.

Total due is current charges plus a late fee itemized only on page 2, and the previous bill was paid, so nothing is carried; reading the gap between current and due on page 1 as a carried balance is the trap. Billed kWh is the metered difference times a multiplier of 60, and the deposit on hand printed on page 2 is neither carried nor due.

A propane ticket that prints the customer's running account balance, over a hundred times the delivery, next to the amount due; the amount due is the delivery, nothing is carried, and the invoice number stands in for the account.

A scanned dyed-diesel ticket (image only) filed with propane: three per-gallon tax lines repeat the fuel quantity, so billed usage is the fuel line alone, not their sum; current charges include those taxes and sales tax, and the invoice number stands in for the account.

One account with three service sections (two meters and area lighting); current charges are the sum of all three and each meter's kWh is its own usage line, so keying lines by account alone loses sections. The previous balance was paid in three payments, so nothing is carried.
